subject: Cognitive Science
title: Motivated Forgetting
description: Learn Motivated Forgetting in one minute.

hook.text: A trauma survivor can't recall details of the event. Did the brain deliberately hit delete?

buildup.text: Freud proposed repression: the unconscious pushes painful memories out of awareness to protect you.

discovery.text: Modern research shows a real mechanism: the think/no-think paradigm lets people suppress specific memories.

twist.text: The prefrontal cortex actively inhibits hippocampal retrieval. Suppression is a measurable brain event.

climax.text: But suppression is imperfect. Suppressed memories can return under stress or the right cue.

punchline.text: You can push memories down. They don't always stay.

quiz.question: What does the think/no-think paradigm demonstrate?
options: People can deliberately suppress specific memories

details.summary: People sometimes forget things they would prefer not to remember. Suppression is the conscious effort to push memories away. Repression, a Freudian concept, is the unconscious burying of traumatic memories.
details.whyItMatters: Motivated forgetting raises profound questions about memory, trauma, and the legal system. The debate over recovered memories has real consequences for therapy and criminal justice.
takeaways: Conscious suppression can reduce memory accessibility
The existence of unconscious repression remains debated
The think/no-think paradigm shows voluntary forgetting is possible

faq.question: Can people really intentionally forget things?
faq.answer: Yes. The think/no-think paradigm shows that repeatedly suppressing a memory when cued reduces later recall. Brain imaging confirms that prefrontal regions actively inhibit hippocampal retrieval during suppression. The effect is modest but reliable across many studies.

faq.question: Are recovered memories of trauma reliable?
faq.answer: This is deeply controversial. Some recovered memories may be genuine, but research shows that false memories can be implanted through suggestion and therapeutic techniques. The scientific consensus is cautious: recovered memories should be treated with care and corroborating evidence sought.
